hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, dark visual features—typically deep black, charcoal, or dark gray—set against a lighter, brighter background of white, silver, or light gray. The activating elements are often organic, rounded, or bounded forms, such as the pupils and dark surrounds of eyes, cavernous facial features (nostrils, open mouths), or the dense silhouettes of animals (bison, dog, bird), all defined by a sharp intensity boundary relative to the illuminated surroundings. The neuron remains invariant to object identity (ranging from animal faces and bodies to human anatomy and inanimate objects), texture, and scale, provided the strong dark-on-light tonal polarity is maintained. The activating feature typically occupies 15–50% of the image area and is generally centered or positioned slightly to the left within the frame.
